gist: The task file implied the dependency diagram is produced automatically, yet no tool exists to build it, so readers could trust a stale hand-kept view.
A fixture described a hostile on-disk folder whose name contains slashes, which cannot exist; it should be framed as an input string rejected before any path is built.
A compressed two-word phrase left unclear that control characters are removed when the gate text is shown back to the user.
A verification tag carried explanatory prose inside its brackets, breaking the pure-tag format that the manual-entry sweep relies on to find entries.
A second verification tag mixed prose into its brackets, so a search for manual entries by exact tag form could skip it.
The index page title used lowercase where sibling doctrine titles use title case.
A cross-reference parenthetical lacked a relative pronoun and could be parsed wrongly.
Concurrency appeared as an example under two separate review lenses, blurring where that concern belongs.
Doctrine text presumed a running pipeline already scans for leaked secrets, though the repository had no automated workflows yet.
The doc stated scripts are already linted and scanned by automation that did not yet exist in the repository.
Guidance told reviewers to discard or lower an unconverged finding, then spoke of it surviving, without saying only lowered ones remain and where they route.
The validation angle list did not say which angles are the required baseline and which are conditional additions.
The readme repeated the same confusing verb agreement about reinstall behaviour that the script comment had.
The documented lookup order assumed a home directory always exists, omitting that home-less setups only resolve through the first two sources.
The doctrine index showed the user-directory fallback as unconditional, though the resolver drops it when no home or override variable is present.
The documented-option parser accepted an empty quoted key, letting a malformed table row count as documentation and weakening the drift check.
A script comment had a subject and verb that read as disagreeing in number, confusing the reinstall behaviour description.
The header listed only two exit statuses, but strict-error mode lets a failing write command surface its own status, often 1.
A comment wrongly promised the pinned permission mask is always at least as strict as the caller's, which fails for masks removing owner bits.
The header implied the home-directory fallback always applies, but the resolver skips it entirely when neither the override variable nor a home is set.
The meta-spec's sample task status values omitted the completion annotation form the bundle already used, so readers could take the list as the full allowed set.
Nested inline-code markers around a worker handle example rendered incorrectly and obscured the intended literal.
A script comment had an extra unmatched closing parenthesis that made the note confusing to read.
An error message was routed through a piped helper process instead of writing to standard error directly, contradicting the script's no-shell-out claim.
A citation list left its second amendment reference without the required kind prefix and date, making it an unrecognized citation form.
Another requirement cited a later amendment without the brief prefix, so the citation kind was ambiguous to parsing.
A citation list qualified only its first amendment reference with the brief prefix and date, leaving the second one ambiguous against the meta-spec's citation rules.
Another citation list left the second amendment reference without its brief prefix and date, so its citation kind was ambiguous under the meta-spec.
The test computed its own location via a directory change inside a substitution without clearing the search-path variable, so stray output could corrupt the path.
The PR summary gave a count of final outcomes that did not match the doc, which defines one fewer and treats the pause as a suspension state.
The doctrine used a nonstandard spelling of a word meaning the ability to undo a change.
Sign-off checklist IDs were said to stay stable when regenerated, but nothing guaranteed it: reverting an earlier marked commit would shift positional numbers.
A missing comma after a closing parenthesis ran the aside into the next list, so the sentence parsed wrongly.
An observation entry was written as a stacked noun phrase that was ungrammatical and did not clearly say which anchor value disagreed with which.
The README said the full check enforces spec validation, but that step only printed a skip notice because the validator script did not exist yet.
The local commit-lint task treated any git failure, such as a missing upstream ref, as an empty range, so linting was skipped without notice.
The script header claimed a strictly portable toolset while the code relied on temp-file and match-only grep utilities outside that standard.
Error output echoed directory names raw, so control bytes in a repo-supplied name could reach CI logs even though header values were already sanitized.
The requirement ID pattern allowed several group letters where the meta-spec permits exactly one, so malformed IDs passed parsing.
The default-baseline probe could print git error text on a ref that exists but does not peel to a commit, so the intended silent skip was noisy.
Baseline ID extraction also accepted multi-letter groups, so renumbering detection could be sidestepped with IDs the meta-spec forbids.
The validator checked the format version header only in the main requirements file, so sibling spec files could omit it or diverge without a finding.
Deleting the authoritative requirements file left the status unset, so an active bundle's errors were downgraded to warnings and the run passed.
Test coverage extraction matched requirement IDs with more than one group letter, so it drifted from the single-letter grammar used elsewhere.
Splitting the directory listing on whitespace let a name with an embedded newline break into fake entries, so the naming check could be dodged.
The symlink pass split its listing the same unsafe way, so a symlink with a newline in its name could slip past the rule against symlinked directories.
The doctrine said each swept file is opened only once, but the code also opens it for a null-byte screen and for digests before and after the parse.
When a bundle had no requirements file, status atoms failed as unknown with no explanatory note, unlike the unreadable and unrecognized cases.
A script comment called the sweep one read of the file, but the screening and digest steps around the single parse each open it again.
The argument hint suggested a free-form name while the body used that argument as a validated spec identifier in paths and branches, and never explained the step between them.
The pre-flight step labeled its input with one term and then validated it as a different kind of value, leaving the argument contract unclear.
A prose line in the skill file ran past the repository's column width convention for markdown text.
Pre-flight only explained validator output for draft bundles, so a failing already-active bundle could be walked through and rejected only at the end.
Sign-off required re-running the validator even though the procedure elsewhere allows it to be missing, leaving that path undefined.
The audit note for a missing validator always claimed a status flip, which is wrong on re-walks of specs that were already active.
Two requirement references dropped their standard prefix, breaking the log's searchable ID convention.
A task note reused the name of a task-state section as an inline label, so readers and tools could misread the task's state.
The description promised the skill never commits, yet its maintenance section has it append to a log and commit.
A possessive pronoun in the front-matter description had an unclear referent, so it could read as describing the worktree.
The intro said a missing repository degrades gracefully while a later step says to halt, so the skill contradicted itself.
The spec name parsed from the branch went into file paths without the identifier charset check sibling skills enforce, so path traversal was possible.
The inference fallback did not say which file holds the status, and it skipped the directory-name check required everywhere else.
The status marker was written in a different form from the exact bold line the spec format defines, so a literal search would miss it.
The single-bundle guess could select a reserved underscore-prefixed accumulator directory as if it were a real spec.
The spec inference covered one or several matches but gave no handling when no candidate bundle existed.
Later steps always read files under the spec directory, even when the branch name gave no valid spec, so they used an undefined path.
The state load showed just one task entry, although a branch can cover a bundle of several tasks.
The fallback text called the loaded context complete even when pull request state could not be read.
A branch with no pull request yet was not treated as a normal partial load, so the lookup failure had no defined handling.
The invariants banned commits and spec-file edits without exempting the drift-log write the maintenance footer requires.
An unmatched closing markup tag was left at the end of the skill file from authoring.
An observation said misplaced task annotations had been fixed, but the task file on the branch still had them under the wrong task.
Exit-code documentation tied status 2 to one missing-file case while the code also returns it for extra arguments and temp-file failures.
Header wording implied literal string matching although the classifier actually uses extended regular expressions with alternation.
Temp file creation for piped input relied on the no-argument form, which some stricter Unix variants reject, contradicting the script's portability promise.
Buffering standard input to a temp file ignored write failures, so a truncated log could be classified instead of failing with an environment error.
A missing container image/tag error was classed as a retryable infrastructure blip, so retries were wasted on a deterministic failure.
The advertised optional argument did not say which forms are accepted, while the validation rule only described a bare identifier.
Subject-verb disagreement in a sentence about several documents failing to resolve.
Skill text kept an outdated internal task-number note about when a doctrine document would arrive, though that document already ships.
Pre-flight steps disagreed on whether a prefixed path or only a bare id may be passed, and left the validate-before-use order implicit.
The skill began reading a config option without the options reference listing it among that option's consumers.
A retryable-only fixture still included the missing-image error, which the classifier now treats as deterministic.
No test checked that the missing-image error outranks a retryable pull-failure match on the same line.
A test comment suggested the classifier's own command line honours a double-dash separator, when that guard only exists internally.
Whole-word matching treated a dot as a boundary, so a longer token sharing the id's prefix wrongly satisfied the changelog check for a superseded requirement.
The id matcher put line anchors inside regex alternations, which some regex engines handle unreliably, so valid changelog mentions could go unmatched.
Supersede check accepted any mention under the changelog heading, including undated text, though the format requires a dated entry.
No regression case proved that an undated changelog mention fails to clear a superseded requirement.
The description field of the worker settings fragment dropped a relative pronoun, making the sentence ungrammatical.
Script-directory resolution passed a double-dash to dirname, which standards do not require it to accept, diverging from the repository's usual form.
An unreadable or unlocatable defaults file returned the ordinary key-absent status with no message, making a broken install look normal.
The broken-install check only tested that the defaults file existed, so a present but unreadable file exited silently like an absent key.
Header claimed the lock protocol exactly matched another script's inline lock, though their failure handling already differed.
Lock script resolved its location with a double-dash dirname call that some platforms may reject, unlike sibling scripts.
The lock script discarded the config reader's stderr, hiding its broken-install warning so the threshold quietly fell back to its default.
A lock-directory creation failure unrelated to contention was reported as a busy lock, hiding real filesystem errors and silently skipping work.
After clearing a stale lock, a failed retry was always treated as contention, masking genuine errors that the first attempt already reported.
A hyphenated term in the header was broken across lines, so it reads as two separate fragments.
An awk diagnostic reached stderr by spawning an external command rather than writing to the stderr device as other repo scripts do.
The watch-mode text used a plural, informal name for a dispatch backend instead of the canonical token used in config and elsewhere.
A readiness test fixture left out a mandatory task field, so it tested a task shape the validator would reject.
The CLI quietly kept only the final positional argument and treated an empty catalog flag as the default catalog rather than rejecting both.
A comment described the parser's intermediate records as tab-delimited while the code actually produced and read pipe-delimited ones.
Value extraction removed only double quotes, so single-quoted or comment-trailed catalog values kept stray characters and silently failed to match.
The catalog reader matched one fixed indentation width, so a reformatted file lost all its entries with no warning.
Field validation skipped breadth entries, so a malformed one was printed as a row with blank columns instead of being warned about and dropped.
The empty-parse warning reused the parser's strict header pattern, so an indented or commented section header yielded no entries and no warning.
The cleanup trap read temp-dir variables before they were assigned, so an early exit under nounset errored in cleanup and obscured the real failure.
Temp directories created in later test sections were never registered with the exit trap, so an aborted run could leave them on disk.
The Python detection test checked only the linter and type checker, so a regression losing formatter or test-runner detection would still pass.
A design decision claimed a requirement only pointed to the protected-document set, yet that requirement repeated the whole list inline.
The brief's summary copy of the protected-document list was stale, lacking an entry that the amendment and the normative spec had already added.
The brief cited a doctrine file without its folder and wrote a requirement ID without its prefix, unlike every other reference in the bundle.
Paired requirement references in the signed record lacked the canonical identifier prefix on one ID.
A changelog heading still said approval was outstanding although the same change set recorded the completed re-walkthrough.
A requirement cross-reference dropped the standard identifier prefix on its second ID, breaking naming consistency and search.
A second paired requirement reference also omitted the identifier prefix on one of its IDs.
The dependency graph labelled a still-planned task as finished even though its section had no completion record.
The doctrine copy of the same sentence also omitted a relative pronoun, so the clause was awkward to parse.
A table row in the brief used a hyphenated spelling of a term the surrounding text spells with a space.
One line hyphenated a term that the rest of the amendment writes as two separate words, hurting search and consistency.
Wording said one pipeline run was met by another run, when the thing being met was the release gate condition.
A sentence lacked a relative pronoun, making it hard to tell which run carries the manual verification pass.
The scoping paragraph for adversarial checking left unstated what applies when a skill declares nothing, unlike the sibling section that spells out its default.
A doctrine summary bullet said a method was favoured in two cases without naming which two, leaving readers to guess.
The brief's top heading did not start with the spec title, breaking the naming pattern every other brief in the repository follows.
Provenance recorded an abbreviated commit hash where sibling briefs store the full one, leaving the anchor ambiguous over time.
Same malformed secret-scanner example in the brief: no subcommand, so a test built from it would not run.
The example secret-scanner command omitted its required subcommand and source flag, so copying it verbatim yields an invalid invocation.
Test plan for degraded input ignored a well-formed scope selector matching nothing, a case the requirement explicitly covers.
Test entry only checked the diagram tool being missing, not installed-but-broken, which the requirement says must degrade identically.
Success output always credited the command-line option for the attestation even when the environment variable supplied it.
A risk note named a nonexistent location for the per-machine override file instead of the one the config loader really reads.
Index citations used bare requirement IDs that collide with another spec's rows; only the decision ID carried its namespace qualifier.
A sentence used a truncated, stuttering form of the document's established term for the shared observation channel.
The containment check accepted absolute candidates lying under the root, while the signed-off contract says any absolute path must be refused.
Failure text blamed a missing parent directory although the resolver also fails on permissions, link read errors, or runaway link chains.
One help line still advertised a generic path argument after the contract moved to root-relative paths only.
The lightweight manifest parser took the first identifier key it saw, so a nested object's value could become the namespace.
Usage text promised an absolute root unconditionally, yet a relative override was echoed back as-is, producing a relative result.
A test's text match for the manifest key also hit a nested author field, so it could pass with no top-level plugin identifier.
No test placed a nested identifier ahead of the top-level one, leaving the parser's wrong-key selection undetected.
The script's dependency note listed fewer external utilities than the code actually calls, so its portability claim was incomplete.
When real paths could not be resolved, the containment gate was silently skipped and file reads proceeded instead of refusing.
The decision lister accepted headings missing the mandated colon, offering IDs the single-decision resolver could never find.
A group-scoped request on a bundle lacking its requirements file printed an empty list rather than saying that file was absent.
The all-decisions guard treated colon-less malformed headings as real, reporting a decision set for a bundle that has none.
One content probe let its search tool's error output through on an unreadable file, unlike its sibling probes that silence it.
A single-decision request on a bundle lacking its design file printed an empty list rather than naming the missing file.
Skill metadata listed the positional argument before the options, disagreeing with the script's usage text and invocation section.
Under errexit, a failing permission reset in the exit trap could stop the trap before the temp directory was removed, skipping cleanup.
Status fallback checked only that a file existed, so a present but unreadable file crashed the header read under errexit instead of degrading.
The file inventory reported an existing but unreadable file as present even though the model could not parse it.
Parsing was attempted on bundle files that existed but could not be read, aborting the run mid-stream instead of skipping them as absent.
Discarding all error output from the overlay-root helper hid its real warnings and made a missing helper look like every overlay was absent.
The missing-resolver warning claimed only core defaults would be used, yet an explicit machine-local override variable was still honored.
With the resolver helper absent or not executable, each overlay lookup printed its own shell error instead of warning once and degrading.
A YAML document marker followed by a trailing comment was flagged as malformed, which could hard-fail a valid shared overlay.
The flatness heuristic accepted top-level sequence entries containing a colon, letting a non-flat overlay slip past the hard-fail policy.
A directory or other non-regular entry at the shared overlay path skipped the malformed check and was quietly treated as missing instead of hard-failing.
A non-regular entry at the machine-local overlay path was silently ignored rather than producing the expected warning and fallback.
The adopter overlay was validated only as a regular file, so a directory there was dropped without the warning the policy requires.
The header implied structurally bad core defaults get a diagnostic, but only a missing or unreadable defaults file was ever reported.
One assertion invoked the command under test a second time just to build its failure text, rather than reusing a captured result.
The header attributed the reveal seam to the wrong design decision, contradicting which decision actually governs that requirement.
Identifier stripping had no word-boundary check, so ID-like fragments inside ordinary words were cut out and corrupted the plain text.
dismissal: It was one of several known latent gaps already logged as deferred in an earlier review handoff, so it was left for later.

gist: A comment promised normative records are numbered in source order, but the code numbers all modals first and thresholds afterward.
dismissal: It was among the latent gaps previously recorded as deferred observations, so the earlier pass chose not to act on it.

gist: The modal-keyword boundary test treated digits as separators, so tokens with a numeric suffix were wrongly tagged as normative.
Piping the model stream with an added newline would emit a spurious blank record for empty input, breaking the empty-in, empty-out contract.
dismissal: It was one of the known latent gaps already logged as a deferred observation by a prior review, so it was not acted on then.

gist: The observation log still described already-resolved translator gaps as open, misstating the current behaviour and what remained.
The test file's index of covered properties omitted the two newest numbered sections.
The filename-to-phrase check looked only for text already in the fixture, so dropping the task-list mapping would not have failed it.
An assertion failed only on emitted output and ignored the checker's exit status, so a crashing check with no output passed silently.
The real-bundle leak check missed bare group references and dotted task numbers, so it enforced less than its stated scrub scope.
The availability guard only checked that the helper file existed, so a helper lacking the run bit skipped the warn-and-fallback path and overlays quietly vanished.
Discarding the helper's stderr hid its own warnings, such as a bad manifest name, so users could not tell why a layer resolved as missing.
The containment test matched secret file text against output that only ever holds a path, so it could never detect a leak and passed vacuously.
The relative-escape test also searched path-only output for secret contents, so a containment breach would go unnoticed.
The explain-mode checks read the exit status after a pipe into a field splitter, so they tested the splitter rather than the resolver and missed failures.
With the layered resolver in place, a missing shipped seed catalog produced an empty merge and zero guards with success, where it used to fail loudly.
A temp file was created without an explicit template under the temp dir, unlike every other script here, putting the stated old-shell portability floor in doubt.
Extra positional arguments following the double-dash separator were silently dropped instead of being rejected as a usage error.
A dangling symlink failed the existence test and counted as an absent layer instead of a malformed one, and suppressed containment errors gave a misleading escape message.
Redirecting straight into the artifact truncated it before assembly ran, so a failed build left an empty or partial file and wiped a previous good one.
The assembler's error output was thrown away, so a failed build showed only a vague generic notice without the real cause.
A test comment contradicted itself by calling one path both tracked and untracked.
A placeholder for the adopter overlay root appeared with no definition or pointer, leaving readers to guess its meaning.
The guide named only the machine-local file as the place for config overrides, leaving out the adopter-level and repo-shared config layers.
The local config file was described as ignored by git unconditionally, though an adopting repo does not inherit those ignore rules.
The secrets note promised machine-local overlays are never committed, but that holds only when the adopting repo's ignore rules cover those directories.
A bare section-six cross-reference pointed at a section this guide lacks, since the intended target was in the overlays document.
The intro offered dispatch isolation as an example overlay preference, while a later section says it is a general core capability.
Documented overlay root paths ended in a slash, while the resolver script prints them without one, so the doc misrepresented actual output.
A heading gave the config resolver's bare file name without its scripts directory, implying it can be run from the search path.
The rule-doc resolver heading omitted the scripts directory that the runnable examples include, so the two forms disagreed.
The catalog resolver heading lacked the scripts directory used in its own examples, making the invocation unclear.
The degradation table promised success status for malformed overlays, yet resolvers still return their usual not-found codes once the remaining layers lack the item.
Body text named the rule-doc resolver without its directory, unlike the rest of the guide.
The guide said the repo's ignore rules skip the overlay directories, contradicting a pattern already in the ignore file.
An observation claimed the repo ignore file missed the local overlay directories, though a wildcard rule already covered them, so it recorded a stale claim.
Decision-map summary text used a different term for the discarded option than the section labels and requirement wording, giving readers inconsistent vocabulary.
A code comment justified omitting the SVG namespace attribute by calling it a network fetch, which is false since namespace URIs are only identifiers.
Label truncation kept one less than the cap and then appended an ellipsis, so shortened labels exceeded the intended maximum length.
The explanatory intro about arrows and columns was emitted before the empty-graph check, so an empty bundle described a diagram that never appears.
Edges whose dependency had no matching task were still sent to the layout probe, which invented phantom nodes and skewed the computed coordinates.
When the external layout tool existed but failed, the rendered note still claimed the tool was absent, misreporting why the fallback layout was used.
A non-integer timeout setting was handed straight to sleep; the watchdog then errored out before killing the layout process, letting it hang indefinitely.
Coordinate checks only verified allowed characters, so malformed numbers like a lone dot or doubled dots passed and were silently coerced into bogus positions.
A test header bullet claimed the failing-tool path behaves identically to absence, yet the note text deliberately differs and is asserted to differ.
An error path printed the caller-supplied selector unfiltered to stderr, letting embedded control bytes tamper with terminal or log output on direct invocation.
The bad requirement-group error repeated the raw selector, so control characters could reach the terminal when the assembler was run directly.
The invalid decision-id message echoed the unsanitized selector, breaking the repository rule that user input is stripped of control bytes before display.
The fallback unknown-selector error printed the raw value, allowing escape sequences to inject into terminal or log output.
Whole-bundle rendering gained an extra standalone model parse even though each view already parses the bundle and one view passes the needed record through.
Graph-only scopes still ran the scoping and translation pipeline whose output they never use, wasting work and inheriting its failures.
A counter variable was initialized in an awk program but never read, leaving dead state that hints at logic that does not exist.
Header usage examples still showed the scope flag as required after the usage function was corrected to mark it optional.
Usage text presented the scope flag as mandatory although the script falls back to a whole-bundle default when it is left out.
The scoping script's selector errors still printed raw input with control characters, a leftover after the same hardening was applied to the assembler.
A test meant to prove framing prose varies compared whole lines including an attribute that always varies, so it passed even with identical prose.
The onboarding guide used a bare-name placeholder for the command argument, implying only a name works when the command also accepts a path.
Timeout documentation suggested fractional values work, but the script only honors whole non-negative seconds and silently resets anything else to the default.
The read-only guarantee was stated absolutely, yet the optional layout probe writes temporary files, so the claim overstated what the command avoids.
The pull request text said a task's ledger state was moved, but the task file was left unchanged, so the description contradicted the diff.
The coverage gate's scoped list of suites left out the integration suite, though its comment claims the list is exhaustive, so requirement labels there would not count.
A requirement driving identifier validation described task ids vaguely rather than stating the exact pattern the repo already defines elsewhere.
A task note cited the wrong risk-register entry for the merge-strategy caveat, pointing at the marker wedge risk instead.
The blocked-case assertion joined its two checks with OR, so a selector that succeeded with empty or wrong output still passed.
The rejection message printed the untrusted ref verbatim, letting control bytes or newlines inject into terminals and logs.
The status table gave severity for three statuses but not the finished one, contradicting the invariant prose just below it.
The doctrine's validator severity sentence left out the finished status, though the validator treats findings there as errors too.
Slash-joined status names in an invariant could be read as either-or rather than excluding both states.
A reworded invariant lost its negation, so it read as forbidding action on the executable statuses instead of on all others.
A changelog line spoke of one supersede annotation while the entry actually adds three of them.
A task's status value began with the pull request state instead of the task's own state, unlike every other task entry.
The options reference named a script without its directory prefix, unlike the other script entries in that table.
A base ref passing the character check but naming no commit was accepted, so later git queries quietly misderived task states.
An inline comment claimed the state-dir override is confined, but the code lets it be any directory and only contains per-task paths.
The pull request listing used the CLI's default page size, so evidence for older tasks was silently dropped once the repo passed that count.
A temp file was created with no name template, breaking the house rule that keeps the call working on BSD-style systems.
An untouched dispatch branch left behind after main advanced looked like merged work, so the task was wrongly derived as completed.
The mainline history walk ran again for each task inside the loop although the base never changes, scaling with tasks times history.
Section headings kept a trailing carriage return in Windows line-ending files, so every task was flagged as outside a known section.
The bad-heading diagnostic printed raw file text, letting control characters from repository content reach CI output.
A later file with findings overwrote an earlier unreadable-input exit status, so the script returned 1 rather than the usage-error code.
Clearing markers always reported success, hiding a failed removal and leaving the marker behind in an otherwise fail-closed script.
When a directory sat at the marker path, the rename moved the temp file inside it and the write reported success with no marker created.
A multi-id marker write that failed partway left the earlier markers in place, so part of a failed batch looked in progress.
The skill doc listed the transient lock as part of the durable dispatch evidence, where the rest of the doc says branch plus marker.
A prose-difference check could pass trivially when the fallback run printed no framing line, because nothing verified that capture was non-empty.
A source-structure regex required exactly two spaces before the case arm, which tied the check to indentation instead of the arm's presence.
An assertion matched text that also appears in a negative halt-list row, so it stayed green even if the gate header stopped naming both statuses.
The conventions doc still promised exact preservation of sticky sections after the same overclaim had been corrected in the script.
The header promised sticky section bodies come through unchanged, yet the emitter strips surrounding whitespace from them.
Unrecognized sections were all moved to the end, so a reconcile would relocate a top-of-file dependency-graph section away from its place.
The documented dedupe-by-id guarantee did not hold for task blocks duplicated inside human-owned or unrecognized sections, which kept every copy.
The final pass squeezes runs of blank lines, which contradicts the documented promise that sticky sections stay untouched.
Nothing checked the temp-file rename's exit status, so a failed move still logged success, returned zero and leaked the temporary file.
A comment overstated the lock-cleanup ordering: a signal arriving after acquisition but before the trap is armed can still leave the lock behind.
The command-line preflight accepted a symlinked ledger, then the inner refusal was swallowed, so the command exited zero without writing.
A stub for resolving a merged PR's head branch existed, but no case exercised that fallback, so the resolution path went untested.
The conflict test left the diff3 base marker out of both the fixture and the assertion, so stripping it was never verified.
The exit-status docs left out the newer refusal path taken when the derivation engine is missing or cannot run.
The header still said the script needs no version control, though selection now calls an engine that requires a repository work tree.
Capturing the engine's error stream together with its records hid warnings the engine prints on runs that still succeed.
The selector kept only task rows from the engine output, so degraded-evidence and contradiction records never reached the operator on success.
An observation said two consumers rely on the engine's ready and blocked states, but neither actually branches on them.
A comment said spec identifiers allow only letters and dashes, leaving out the digits the engine also accepts.
A test helper made one commit per completed dependency in every case, slowing the suite when one commit carrying all the trailers would do.
The state doc defined the dispatch evidence two different ways in separate sections (lock-based versus marker-based), leaving readers unsure which holds.
The doc named an ancestry git command for reachability that the state script never runs; the script counts commits ahead and checks first-parent history.
The doc implied the advisory lock lives with the marker directory, when it actually sits at its own path in the spec directory.
The single-writer section still said the task skill writes status lines after the change removed that write.
The doc said a missing hosting CLI emits a degradation record, but the script quietly treats that case like having no remote.
The step text credited the reconcile with writing the status annotation, but the reconcile only keeps annotations and decides section placement.
The procedure wrote an in-progress status assuming the reconcile had already moved the block; a reconcile skipped on a busy lock leaves a ledger contradiction.
Skill prose said the reconcile script owns both block placement and the status line, yet the script only moves sections and leaves annotations alone.
Test header described the reconcile as writing status text, contradicting the sync script, which only places sections and keeps per-task annotations as-is.
A leftover comment and failure message still called the reconcile the status author after the header was corrected, and the grep missed the bold markdown form.
An assertion required skill wording that over-claimed what the reconcile does, so passing the test meant keeping inaccurate prose.
The activity-date check matched the phrase anywhere in the skill, so it stayed green even if the intended PR step dropped that instruction.
A repeated task id let its final occurrence override an earlier sticky-section sighting, which could skew the derived bundle state.
Testing for a regular file before testing for a link let dangling or directory-pointing links pass as absent files, skipping the refusal and its diagnostic.
The authoritative requirements file was read through a link without refusal, so its siblings got updated while the linked file itself was skipped, splitting state.
The status function's comment said failures get logged, yet its derivation-failure branches return success quietly and the caller never logs them.
Once the primary file reached Done, later runs exited early, so a sibling left behind by an earlier refused write could never be brought back in line.
The placement docstring promised an untouched tasks file on failure, but the status rewrite runs earlier and is not undone when placement later aborts.
Misspelled word in an observation note where the author meant that changing the anchor script alters every stored anchor.
Comment called the reconcile the only header writer, then right after credited the kickoff skill with one header transition, contradicting itself.
A helper's comment shifted its positional arguments by one, labelling the directory argument as the status value.
